This is an experiment run through multiple rounds. Each round has 10 customers, who face two options £2 and £2.1 per mile. At the end of each round, we decide how many customers face the £2 and the £2.1 rates in the next round. Today we'll stop at 3 rounds, and that will be the experiment concluded. At the end of the experiment, we could optionally calculate the price elasticity of demand --- which is beyond the scope of this module, but still an interesting way to connect data analysis techniques to economics concepts.

## Overview

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(123)
```

To do this problem sheet, we're going to take 5 steps.

1.  Plot the theoretical Prior Beta distributions for £2 and £2.1 price treatments using observed successes and failures of the 2 price point treatments.
2.  Pick out 100,000 values from each Prior Beta distribution for £2 and £2.1. Combine it into 100,000 pairs of picks (also known as) draws.
3.  Make a scatter plot with the draw corresponding to £2 on the horizontal axis, and £2.1 on the vertical axis.
4.  Use the Thompson sampling method to update the treatment probabilities.
5.  Observe the successes and failures of each price offering under the treatment probability.

After step 5, we update our prior distributions and conduct the next round of experiments, following steps 1-5 again.

As a matter of definition, the updated priors are called a posterior after step 5. But called a prior when we go back to step 1.

The following section has code that writes up steps 1 to 5 in detail so that the R knows exactly what to do. Then instead of writing this long code for each round of experimentation, You may skip this section entirely during your studies. However, if you like taking notes while studying, you may read these code blocks and try to summarize for yourself the logic of what we do in today's problem sets. That will be a guaranteed way to learn Adaptive Randomized Controlled Trials. I have provided comments on the code for it to be helpful.

1.  Plot the theoretical Prior Beta distributions for £2 and £2.1 price treatments using observed successes and failures of the 2 price point treatments.

```{r function-plot-beta-theoretical}

# Store success and failures across rounds in a unified dataset
beta_history <- data.frame(
  roundnum = integer(),
  price = character(),
  successes = integer(),
  failures = integer()
)

# define the function to plot theoretical beta distributions
plot_beta_distributions <- function(
    roundnum,
    numsuccess_gbp2,
    numfailure_gbp2,
    numsuccess_gbp2pt1,
    numfailure_gbp2pt1
) {

  # Store the current round's successes and failures  
  current_round <- data.frame(
    roundnum = rep(roundnum, 2),
    price = c("gbp2", "gbp2pt1"),
    successes = c(numsuccess_gbp2, numsuccess_gbp2pt1),
    failures = c(numfailure_gbp2, numfailure_gbp2pt1)
  )

  # Update stored history of successeses and failures with current round's results
  beta_history <<- rbind(
    beta_history[beta_history$roundnum != roundnum, ],
    current_round
  )

  # Use all rounds up to the current round
  history <- beta_history[
    beta_history$roundnum <= roundnum, 
  ]

  # Generate theoretical Beta density values in multiple steps
  # Step a: define values for the x axis on the beta distribution ranging from 0-1 at 1/1000 intervals
  p <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)
  
  # step b: calculate beta distribution using values from the rounds
  density_data <- do.call(
    rbind,
    lapply(seq_len(nrow(history)), function(i) {
      
      # define the 2 parameters for the beta distribution 
      alpha <- history$successes[i] + 1
      beta <- history$failures[i] + 1

      data.frame(
        # define variable: probability (of acceptance) for the x axis of the distribution
        probability = p,
        # define variable: density which is the theoretical beta density value
        density = dbeta(p, alpha, beta),
        price = history$price[i],
        roundnum = history$roundnum[i],
        # define and calculate the mean value of the beta distribution
        mean = alpha / (alpha + beta)
      )
    })
  )


  # attach labels to the 2 treatments so that it appears nicely on the graph 
  density_data$price <- factor(
    density_data$price,
    levels = c("gbp2", "gbp2pt1"),
    labels = c("£2", "£2.1")
  )


  # Define visual properties for each round: lighter shades for early rounds, and dark shades for more recent rounds
  round_widths <- seq(0.7, 1.4, length.out = roundnum + 1)
  round_alphas <- seq(0.2, 1, length.out = roundnum + 2)[-1]
  
  names(round_widths) <- as.character(0:roundnum)
  names(round_alphas) <- as.character(0:roundnum)
  
  # Only show mean lines for the current round
  current_means <- unique(
    density_data[
      density_data$roundnum == roundnum,
      c("price", "roundnum", "mean")
    ]
  )
  
  # draw the theoretical density plot using the data collected above
  ggplot(
    density_data,
    aes(
      x = probability,
      y = density,
      colour = price,
      linetype = price,
      alpha = factor(roundnum),
      linewidth = factor(roundnum),
      group = interaction(price, roundnum)
    )
  ) +
    scale_linetype_manual(
      values = c(
        "£2" = "solid",
        "£2.1" = "longdash"
      ),
      name = "Price"
    ) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_vline(
      data = current_means,
      aes(
        xintercept = mean,
        colour = price
      ),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      linetype = "dashed",
      linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    scale_colour_manual(
      values = c(
        "£2" = "#0072B2",
        "£2.1" = "#D55E00"
      )
    ) +
    scale_alpha_manual(
      values = round_alphas,
      name = "Round"
    ) +
    scale_linewidth_manual(
      values = round_widths,
      name = "Round"
    ) +
    guides(
      alpha = guide_legend(
        title = "Round"
      ),
      linewidth = guide_legend(
        title = "Round"
      )
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste(
        "Posterior Distributions After Round",
        roundnum
      ),
      x = "Acceptance probability",
      y = "Density",
      colour = "Price"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
}
```

2.  Pick out 100,000 values from each Prior Beta distribution for £2 and £2.1. Combine it into 100,000 pairs of picks (also known as) draws.
3.  Make a scatter plot with the draw corresponding to £2 on the horizontal axis, and £2.1 on the vertical axis.

```{r function-plot-beta-pairs}

plot_beta_pairs <- function(
    numdraws,
    numsuccess_gbp2,
    numfailure_gbp2,
    numsuccess_gbp2pt1,
    numfailure_gbp2pt1
) {

  # Draw samples from the two posterior Beta distributions
  draw_gbp2 <- rbeta(
    numdraws,
    numsuccess_gbp2 + 1,
    numfailure_gbp2 + 1
  )

  draw_gbp2pt1 <- rbeta(
    numdraws,
    numsuccess_gbp2pt1 + 1,
    numfailure_gbp2pt1 + 1
  )

  # Combine draws
  pairs <- data.frame(
    draw_gbp2 = draw_gbp2,
    draw_gbp2pt1 = draw_gbp2pt1
  )

  # Identify which treatment wins each pair
  pairs$winner <- ifelse(
    pairs$draw_gbp2 > pairs$draw_gbp2pt1,
    "£2", "£2.1"
  )

  # Calculate probabilities of each treatment winning
  prob_gbp2 <- mean(pairs$winner == "£2")
  prob_gbp2pt1 <- 1 - prob_gbp2

  # Create subtitle
  subtitle_text <- sprintf(
    "Probability that £2 is preferred: %.2f%%; £2.1 is preferred: %.2f%%",
    100 * prob_gbp2,
    100 * prob_gbp2pt1
  )

  # Determine overall winning treatment
  if (prob_gbp2 > 0.5) {

    # £2 wins: blue below diagonal, grey above
    pairs$point_colour <- ifelse(
      pairs$winner == "£2",
      "#0072B2",
      "grey75"
    )

  } else if (prob_gbp2 < 0.5) {

    # £2.1 wins: vermilion above diagonal, grey below
    pairs$point_colour <- ifelse(
      pairs$winner == "£2.1",
      "#D55E00",
      "grey75"
    )

  } else {

    # Exact 50-50 tie: all points grey
    pairs$point_colour <- "grey75"

  }

  # Plot simulated posterior pairs
  ggplot(
    pairs,
    aes(x = draw_gbp2, y = draw_gbp2pt1)
  ) +

    geom_point(
      aes(colour = point_colour),
      alpha = 0.12,
      size = 0.5
    ) +

    # 45-degree reference line
    geom_abline(
      slope = 1,
      intercept = 0,
      colour = "black",
      linewidth = 0.8,
      linetype = "dashed"
    ) +

    # Use exact point colours
    scale_colour_identity() +

    coord_equal(
      xlim = c(0, 1),
      ylim = c(0, 1),
      expand = FALSE
    ) +

    labs(
      title = "Simulated Posterior Pairs",
      subtitle = subtitle_text,
      x = "Acceptance probability (£2)",
      y = "Acceptance probability (£2.1)"
    ) +

    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +

    theme(
      legend.position = "none"
    )
}


```

4.  Use the Thompson sampling method to update the treatment probabilities.
5.  Observe the successes and failures of each price offering under the treatment probability.

## 1. Uniform prior

A Beta distribution can be written as Beta(s+1, f+1). In the Beta-Bernoulli model (a type of Adaptive RCTs that you studied in the lectures), what does s and f stand for?

A standard uniform distribution can be written as U[0,1]. It can also be written as Beta distribution. What would be the s and f in that case?

We have a £2 and £2.1 treatment. Fill the s and f for a uniform prior.

)
```

  numsuccess_gbp2 = 0,
  numfailure_gbp2 = 0,
  numsuccess_gbp2pt1 = 0,
  numfailure_gbp2pt1 = 0
)
```

What is the idea behind Thompson sampling? It is a rule that helps us choose the probabilities for the treatments in the next round based on the last round's results.

It says that Probability(user sees option k in the next round) = Prob(\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_).
